newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS - Ailing Russian planemaker plans layoffs.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Ailing Russian planemaker plans layoffs.

text.p: A major Russian planemaker is to sack 2,000 staff and cut pay for two thirds of its 13,000 workers because it has not sold a single plane all year, a senior company official said on Wednesday.

Vladimir Ryzhkov, Deputy Chief Executive at AO Aviakor, said the company, which makes the workhorse Tupolev-154 passenger jet, had delivered nine planes last year, compared with 78 in the peak production year of 1981.
"We have informed the Federal Employment Service about plans to sack about 2,000 people," Ryzhkov said by telephone from the company's headquarters in the Volga city of Samara.

"We have 28 contracts, but customers do not pay for aircraft," Ryzhkov said, adding that the plant was completing the assembly of three Tu-154s for Czech, Ukrainian and Siberian airlines. One Tu-154 jet costs $13 million.

Aviakor is one of three plants making Tupolev jets, the mainstay of most of Russia's 300-plus airlines. The other plants are in Ulyanovsk, also on the Volga, and in the autonomous region of Tatarstan.
But Tupolev and other Russian firms are finding it hard to compete with quieter and more fuel-efficient Western planes and more than 40 Western-made aircraft are operating in Russia.
That is still tiny compared to the 2,025 planes built in the former Soviet Union and flying here.
A source at the Russian transportation ministry said cash-starved Russian airlines had bought only eight passenger and cargo planes this year.
"Airlines cannot buy new planes due to lack of money," he said. "On the other hand, there is no leasing system for aircraft yet and that would help carriers replace outdated planes."
Yevgeny Shaposhnikov, director of the state-owned Aeroflot airline said on Tuesday that many Western companies were setting tough noise restrictions which would limit the use of Russian planes.
"German authorities are seeking bans on night flying by Russian planes because they are too noisy," Interfax news agency quoted him as saying.
New safety demands by U.S. authorities could restrict Russian planes' passage over the north Atlantic, he added.
Aeroflot said last month it would buy 10 Boeing 737 jets this year to replace Tupolev-134 jets, an announcement which provoked fierce criticism from domestic plane makers.
